title: QMA versus \(\mathrm{QMA}_1\) over Clifford+T
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) for the exact gate set \(\mathcal G=\{H,\mathrm{CNOT},T\}\) defined below? Both classes concern promise problems on finite binary strings and use polynomial-size, uniformly generated verification circuits with polynomially many witness qubits. In \(\mathrm{QMA}\), every yes-instance has a witness accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); in \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\), it has a witness accepted with probability exactly \(1\). In both classes, every witness for a no-instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The one-sided class in this question is explicitly the Clifford+T version.

source_formulation.text: Can bounded-error QMA verification be made perfectly complete?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question, specialized to the explicitly selected exact Clifford+T gate set

why: This determines whether certainty on yes-instances changes the power of efficient quantum proof verification. It separates arbitrarily reliable verification from exact acceptance and affects the relation between quantum satisfiability and general quantum witness problems.
status_note: Matching fresh solution claims found on 16 September 2026. Grewal–Rudolph arXiv:2609.13032v1, submitted 11 September, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 explicitly claim QMA with perfect completeness over a fixed finite gate set and its exact implementation in Clifford+T. Liu–Vidick arXiv:2609.15926v1, submitted 14 September, gives a second claimed construction over {H,X,Toffoli,S}; its stated fixed gates admit exact Clifford+T implementations. These are ordinary finite-register, single-witness claims, so the selected gate set does not protect this target from the new results. The full PDFs and theorem/model scope were inspected, but the complete proofs were not independently certified or checked in Lean. Status is uncertain pending verification, superseding the earlier source-open assessment.

sentences: A perfectly complete quantum proof system accepts some valid witness with probability exactly one.
This question asks whether every QMA proof system can achieve that guarantee without sacrificing efficient verification or soundness.
Approximate gate synthesis creates a special difficulty because a tiny implementation error can destroy exact acceptance.
Two September 2026 preprints now claim finite-register perfect completeness with fixed gates that cover this card’s exact Clifford+T model.
Their stated results match the target, whose status is uncertain pending independent proof verification.

definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). The input length is \(n=|x|\). No acceptance condition is imposed on strings outside the promise. For a fixed problem, a deterministic classical algorithm, on input \(x\), produces a quantum verification circuit \(V_x\) in time polynomial in \(n\). Its witness register \(W\) has \(m(n)\) qubits and its private ancillary register \(A\) has \(a(n)\ge1\) qubits, where \(m,a\) are polynomially bounded integer functions. Circuit size is also polynomially bounded. All bounds and the generating algorithm are fixed for the problem, independently of the particular input.

A qubit is \(\mathbb C^2\) with basis \(|0\rangle,|1\rangle\). A witness is any density matrix \(\rho\) on \(W=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m(n)}\): it is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and has trace one. Hermitian means \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\). Its entries may be arbitrary complex numbers; no efficient preparation or finite classical description of the witness is required. All private ancillas start in \(|0\rangle^{\otimes a(n)}\), uncorrelated with the witness. There is one witness message and no interaction, oracle, preshared resource or nonuniform advice.

The allowed unitary gates, applied to specified wires, are \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,c\oplus b\rangle,\] where \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). These exact matrices define the finite gate set; arbitrary real rotations are not allowed as single gates. A circuit is a finite product of these gates, tensored with identity on all other wires. One designated output qubit is measured in the displayed basis, with outcome one meaning accept. Equivalently, with \(\Pi_{\mathrm{acc}}\) the orthogonal projector onto output value one, its acceptance probability is \[p_x(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_{\mathrm{acc}}V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes|0^{a(n)}\rangle\langle0^{a(n)}|\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right].\]

The verifier is a QMA verifier if \(\forall x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\ \exists\rho:\ p_x(\rho)\ge2/3\) and \(\forall x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\ \forall\rho:\ p_x(\rho)\le1/3\). Using this fixed universal gate set gives the usual bounded-error class QMA. The class \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) changes only the first acceptance requirement to \(p_x(\rho)=1\), retaining all other resources and the same exact gate set. The accepting witness can depend on the yes-input. It need not be accepted by the original QMA verifier with probability one; equality of classes permits a different verifier and polynomial witness length. All registers remain finite and polynomial in input length. Acceptance approaching one through a sequence of circuits is not perfect completeness unless one admissible circuit family attains one exactly.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that every QMA promise problem has a verifier in \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\) under these exact conventions, or a complete Lean-checked proof that some QMA promise problem has no such verifier. The reverse inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}\) is immediate from the acceptance bounds, so the issue is the stated containment or its failure. A negative proof must rule out every eligible one-sided verifier for the separating promise problem, not only one attempted amplification procedure. Exponentially or doubly exponentially small completeness error still differs from zero. Perfect completeness using an infinite register, extra interaction, a different exact gate set without a suitable equivalence proof, or an added oracle does not establish the target. Numerical approximation to the acceptance probability cannot replace this exact yes/no assertion.

context_blocks.text: Editorial gate-set choice: the source treats a family of exact-gate versions of QMA with perfect completeness. This card now fixes Hadamard, CNOT and T, as explicitly selected on 16 September 2026. It does not assert that every other exact-gate version defines the same one-sided class.

A quantum witness can make a yes-instance convincing without being efficiently preparable. Perfect completeness asks whether at least one witness can be accepted with certainty, while keeping every no-instance resistant to all witnesses. The question is about the power of proof systems, not reliability of an experimental device.

Approximate gate synthesis preserves a bounded acceptance gap after allowing sufficiently small error. It does not automatically preserve an acceptance probability equal to one. This is why the source attaches an explicit exact gate set to the one-sided class.

The source proves containment and completeness results for finite gate sets with entries in specified cyclotomic fields, which are fields generated by selected roots of unity. These results clarify exact-gate conventions and quantum satisfiability, but explicitly leave equality with bounded-error QMA open in that earlier source; the September preprints make matching new claims.

Aaronson constructs a quantum oracle relative to which QMA and its perfectly complete version differ. An oracle supplies an additional unitary operation; that theorem does not separate the ordinary classes with only the gates in this card.

Jeffery and Witteveen obtain perfect completeness when the witness system includes an infinite counter register with shift access. Their finite-dimensional truncation instead yields exceptionally small positive completeness error. Neither conclusion gives exact acceptance one with polynomially many ordinary qubits in the selected model.

The source also recalls perfect-completeness results for classical-witness quantum verification and for interactive quantum proofs. A restriction to classical witnesses or the addition of verifier-prover messages changes the model, so those equalities do not settle this single-message quantum-witness question.

Grewal and Rudolph's preprint of 11 September 2026 claims \(\mathrm{QMA}=\mathrm{QMA}_1^{\mathcal G_2}\) for \(\mathcal G_2=\{X,\mathrm{CNOT},\mathrm{Toffoli},H\otimes H\}\). Corollary 1.2 transfers the claimed equality to any gate set implementing these gates exactly with clean ancillas, and the text explicitly includes Clifford+T. Thus this is a matching claim for the exact gate set in the card, not only an equality using arbitrary rotations or an infinite counter. The proof is not independently certified in this review.

Liu and Vidick's preprint of 14 September 2026 separately claims perfect completeness for QMA over \(\{H,X,\mathrm{Toffoli},S\}\), where \(S=\operatorname{diag}(1,i)\), in Theorem 1.3. The model uses finite polynomial resources. Its gates have exact Clifford+T implementations, preserving acceptance probability one; the claimed constant soundness gap permits the usual exact Boolean error reduction. The same paper treats two-message proof systems in separate theorems. Those stronger interaction claims should not be confused with, or substituted for, its one-message QMA theorem.
